name: Water heating

seoDesc: Water heating: work out efficiency from the initial temperature and the heat ice. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: efficiency is what the Water heating calculator works out, and it gets there from the initial temperature, the heat ice, the temperature difference and the heating power. sections.title: How does the Water heating calculator work?
sections.html:
The Water heating calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports efficiency in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the initial temperature, the heat ice, the temperature difference and the heating power.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Water heating calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Efficiency=total energy ÷ (heating power × time)
Final temperature=initial temperature + temperature difference
Heat liquid=(419 ÷ 2) × mass or volume of water × (-20 × final temperature × (final temperature) + 20 × initial temperature × (initial temperature) + 20 × temperature difference − 5463 × (initial temperature) + 7463 × (final temperature)) × (initial temperature, final temperature)
Mass or volume of water=5 × heat ice ÷ (-10540 × initial temperature × (initial temperature) + 2879001 × (initial temperature) + 1670000 × (initial temperature, final temperature))
Mass or volume of water=5 × heat vapor ÷ (9980 × final temperature × (final temperature) + 11323525 × (initial temperature, final temperature) − 3724037 × (final temperature))
Heat liquid=-heat ice − heat vapor + total energy

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Total energy = 10 J, Heating power = 10 W and Time = 10 hrs. Working through the relationship above gives Efficiency = 12 %.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Efficiency = 12 % should be roughly the size you expected from Total energy = 10 J and Heating power = 10 W.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Volume & mass mixed, opening in kilograms
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Energy, opening in joules
  • Energy, opening in joules
  • Energy, opening in joules
  • Energy, opening in joules
  • Temperature change, opening in Celsius

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Water heating calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the initial temperature, the heat ice and the temperature difference — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Water heating calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns efficiency, derived from the initial temperature, the heat ice and the temperature difference. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Water heating calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial temperature, the heat ice, the temperature difference and the heating power, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mass or volume of water in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mass or volume of water opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 22 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Efficiency = 12 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Water heating calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
